title: ‘How to Rob a Bank’ gives a lesson on making an enjoyable heist flick
text:
'How to Rob a Bank' is a diverting actioner with a Robin Hood twist

 Nicholas Hoult and Pete Davidson star in this dark comedy about bank robbers going viral.
 Print this Article 
 View Comments The heist squad in "How to Rob a Bank." Amazon MGM Studios “How to Rob a Bank” is a heist movie that’s three parts “Robin Hood” and two parts “Bonnie and Clyde.” Ryan (Nicholas Hoult from “ Superman ”) leads a team of masked bank robbers on carefully planned hits of small to mid-size banks. After each successful robbery, the crew hits YouTube to promote their latest caper using clips they filmed. The host of these videos wears a wolf mask while giving advice on how to rob banks. Tips include surviving police interrogations and dismantling exploding dye packs. 
 There’s also a primer on how the bank’s money is insured by the FDIC, so any stolen funds will be replaced. The way these antiheroes pitch it, it’s a guilt-free way of sticking it to a corrupt system designed to keep the working class down. “What’s more powerful than a gun?” asks the Big Bad Wolf. 
 “An audience,” he replies. 
 Get Starting Point A guide through the most important stories of the morning, delivered Monday through Friday. Enter Email Sign Up From left: Rhenzy Feliz as Hugo, Pete Davidson as Vince, and Nicholas Hoult as Ryan. Megan Schoenbachler/Amazon MGM Studios Wolfie — or should I say Ryan — is right. As his alter ego, he has narrated 61 videos, which have gone viral with 900 million views and inspired a movement that includes an occasional copycat crime. His crew includes girlfriend Emi (“ Shogun ”’s Anna Sawai), tech whiz Hugo (Rhenzy Feliz), and family man Vince (former “SNL” veteran Pete Davidson ). They’re a contemporary Barrow Gang whose reputation grows through the low-attention span flash and pizazz of a TikTok reel rather than folk songs or newspaper clippings. 
 As in Warren Beatty’s 1967 heist classic, this version of the Barrow gang’s humiliation of a lawman will come back to bite them. That lawman is an FBI agent named John West. West is played by John C. Reilly, perfect casting for a character we’re conflicted about rooting for in this story. Even in his most sinister registers, Reilly somehow emits a ray of likability. Screenwriter Mark Bianculli makes him an amenable, empathetic schlub, but never lets us forget he’s still the law. 
 Zoë Kravitz as Reagan and John C. Reilly as Agent West in "How to Rob a Bank." Amazon MGM Studios Frustrated by his organization’s inability to capture the Big Bad Wolf’s crew, West turns to Reagan (Zoë Kravitz), a hacker on house arrest for writing software that resulted in someone doxxing a federal judge. She called the product FYPOS (an acronym whose meaning is too profane to publish here). Her original intent was stalking her ex-boyfriend using AI to figure out his location. West thinks she can be of use as a tracker; their chatty relationship forms the buddy cop portion of “How to Rob a Bank.” 
 The line between good and bad guys is blurred to the point where you can’t say that there are any true blue heroes. However, there is one incontrovertible villain, Walton, a bank CEO played by a hissable, sleazy Christian Slater. His bank is the one institution the gang refused to hit because it was too big. 
 Rhenzy Feliz as Hugo. Megan Schoenbachler/Amazon MGM Studios Once director David Leitch ( “The Fall Guy” ) gets the heavily stylized, somewhat annoying quick cut, video-mimicking first hour out of his system, “How to Rob a Bank” settles into a more enjoyable standard actioner. The requisite car chases and narrow escapes are balanced by the backstories of all the members of the Big Bad Wolf crew. It’s hard to disagree with their anger at a system that makes rich people richer at the expense of everyone else, and their donations to charities give them a hint of nobility. 
 But as in every heist movie you’ve seen, somebody is bound to make a mistake or turn on the team. This film adds a few welcome twists to those scenarios, building to a climactic high stakes battle that is best described as organized chaos tempered with genuine emotion. 
 Anna Sawai as Emi. Megan Schoenbachler/Amazon MGM Studios Hoult, who is in the running to play 007 , continues to be a charismatic figure onscreen. At times, Ryan wears black eye makeup reminiscent of Hoult’s character Nux in “Mad Max: Fury Road.” Ryan has the same faith in his actions that Nux did, though there’s no Valhalla for this wounded character. 
 As Emi, Sawai is given much more to do than the usual girlfriend role allows. Feliz brings a palpable glee as the crew’s hype man. And Davidson is shockingly good as a tragic figure of sorts, a man for whom the stakes are highest. 
 Pete Davidson as Vince. Megan Schoenbachler/Amazon MGM Studios If there’s a weak link, it’s Kravitz. I don’t know if her laissez-faire take on the character is because Reagan is perpetually high on weed or because Kravitz is disinterested. While she has a give-and-take comic chemistry with Reilly, he’s doing the heavy lifting in their scenes. 
 Though it raises more questions than it can answer, “How to Rob a Bank” is still a fun, diverting fable about getting one over on the man. It would make a great double feature with F. Gary Gray’s superior 1996 Queen Latifah heist movie, “Set It Off.” Like that film, this one doesn’t forget that, while risk often brings rewards, the house always wins. 
 ★★★ 
 HOW TO ROB A BANK 
 Directed by David Leitch. Written by Mark Bianculli. Starring Nicholas Hoult, John C. Reilly, Zoë Kravitz, Pete Davidson, Anna Sawai, Rhenzy Feliz, Christian Slater. At AMC Boston Common, Alamo Drafthouse Seaport, AMC Causeway, suburbs. 122 minutes. R (the usual shootouts and cuss outs) 
 Odie Henderson is the Boston Globe's film critic.
